stances.claim: Public reactions to the SC and judiciary follow a 'selective applause / lampoon' pattern based on whether each ruling matches the public's current preference -- and while fair comment is part of free speech, comments should be 'factually true and legally correct,' not knee-jerk media grabs that injure public trust.

Elected officials are properly responsive to popular sentiment because that is their accountability mechanism -- but magistrates operate in 'a world of reason where logic, evidence, and conscience are their only yardsticks,' sourcing legitimacy from the people's ratification of the Constitution rather than ongoing electoral approval.

Permanency of tenure and constitutional independence are the 'rare luxuries' that enable jurists to decide free of electoral or presidential fear -- to write and act on what others think correct but lack courage to do.
stances.rhetorical_move: structural-protection framing (tenure + independence as enabling, not privilege)

stances.claim: Litigation is decided by reasoned arguments from legal principles and precedents -- not by vote counts, political palatability, friendship, pecuniary considerations, or 'diplomatic quid pro quo' ('I will vote with you in this case, provided you vote with me in this other case').

The Court depends on public faith and trust because it cannot enforce its own pronouncements -- 'It does not command the army, the police, or the raging mob' -- but its dependency is on 'long-term public trust in the institution,' not the 'shifting winds of public opinion.'
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-credibility framing with long-vs-short-term trust distinction

stances.claim: Following Felix Frankfurter, the SC is 'the conscience of society' -- and 'the test of the magistrates' mettle is their capacity to stand by their convictions' against executive, legislators, and 'the mob' that may threaten their families and chant hate slogans.

Beyond being the conscience of society, the unelected SC is also 'the last bastion of democracy and the ultimate defender of the people's rights enshrined in the Constitution' -- and citizens have a duty to help it remain faithful to these expectations.
stances.confidence: asserted as CJ's personal extension of Frankfurter

notable_anecdotes: Three case-pair examples of selective applause/lampoon: (1) De Lima acquittal (RTC Muntinlupa Br. 204, Judge Alcantara) won critics' praise; same RTC's bail denial (Br. 256, Judge Buenaventura) drew their condemnation. (2) SC disbarred Larry Gadon to applause; but its earlier habeas corpus release of Gigi Reyes drew boos. (3) Sandiganbayan plunder conviction of Estrada thunderously applauded; SC's subsequent allowance for him to run for and win as Manila mayor (after Arroyo's pardon) lampooned.
Anti-quid-pro-quo formulation reproduced verbatim ('I will vote with you in this case, provided you vote with me in this other case') as the kind of bargain the judiciary must not make.
'It does not command the army, the police, or the raging mob' -- the most-cited line in CJ's writing on judicial power.
Felix Frankfurter cited as the source for the 'conscience of society' framing -- a US Supreme Court Justice's idiom imported into PH discourse.

List of pressures jurists must withstand: 'tyrants, lynch mobs, and even the best-intentioned but ill-informed crusaders' -- the third item is the most unusual, putting well-meaning critics into the same category as tyrants when they are wrong on the law.

The Court's prayer-list: 'courage, integrity, and sagacity' -- three virtues as the only tools -- contrasted with what it does not desire: 'the brute power of the executive' or 'the patronage of the legislature.'

CJ's elevation beyond Frankfurter: 'the unelected Supreme Court is not merely the conscience of society; it is also the last bastion of democracy and the ultimate defender of the people's rights' -- a stronger formulation than Frankfurter's original.
Citizen-duty closer: 'Our duty as citizens is to help the Court and the judiciary remain faithful to these high expectations.'

one_paragraph_summary: Diagnosing the selective applause / lampoon pattern in PH public reactions to the SC and lower judiciary -- Judge Alcantara's RTC Muntinlupa Branch 204 acquittal of former Senator Leila de Lima drew critics' praise but the same RTC's Branch 256 (Judge Buenaventura) denial of her bail drew condemnation; the SC's disbarment of Larry Gadon was applauded while its earlier habeas corpus release of Jessica 'Gigi' Reyes drew boos; the Sandiganbayan's plunder conviction of Joseph Estrada was thunderously applauded while the SC's later allowance for him to run for Manila mayor after Arroyo's pardon was lampooned -- Panganiban argues that while fair comment is part of free speech, comments should be 'factually true and legally correct,' not knee-jerk reactions and opportunistic media grabs that 'serve transitory glory but injure public trust in the courts.' Members of Congress and Cabinet officials properly respond to current popular sentiment because that is their accountability mechanism, but 'magistrates must live in a world of reason where logic, evidence, and conscience are their only yardsticks,' sourcing legitimacy from the Constitution ratified overwhelmingly by the people rather than ongoing electoral approval. Permanency of tenure and constitutional independence are the 'rare luxuries' that excise jurists from parochial ties and enable consistent objective decision-making free of electoral fear or presidential rebuff. Cases are won or lost by reasoned arguments from legal principles and precedents -- not by votes, palatability, friendship, pecuniary considerations, or 'diplomatic quid pro quo' ('I will vote with you in this case, provided you vote with me in this other case'). The Court depends on public faith because 'it does not command the army, the police, or the raging mob' -- but its dependency is on 'long-term public trust in the institution,' not 'the shifting winds of public opinion.' Quoting the late US Justice Felix Frankfurter that the SC is 'the conscience of society,' CJ stresses that the test of magistrates' mettle is their capacity to stand by their convictions when executive, legislators, and the mob 'rage against them, threaten their families, and chant slogans of hate.' The Court 'does not lust for the brute power of the executive,' nor desire 'the patronage of the legislature' -- it 'prays only for courage, integrity, and sagacity.' He then elevates Frankfurter's formulation: 'the unelected Supreme Court is not merely the conscience of society; it is also the last bastion of democracy and the ultimate defender of the people's rights enshrined in the Constitution.' He closes with the citizen-duty completion: 'Our duty as citizens is to help the Court and the judiciary remain faithful to these high expectations.'
